one_liner: Single-pass AVX/AVX-512 min and max for float32 and int16 NumPy arrays, replacing separate np.amin and np.amax passes.
what_it_does: One function, numpy_minmax.minmax(a), returns (min, max) as NumPy scalars for an array in one call. A cffi extension runs a C kernel for float32 arrays that are C- or F-contiguous or 1-D strided (including negative strides) and for contiguous int16 arrays; every other dtype or layout falls back to np.amin(a), np.amax(a). There is no axis, keepdims, out or where argument, and empty arrays raise ValueError as NumPy does.
how_it_is_fast: Pass fusion: one sweep over memory updates both a running-min and a running-max vector (_mm256_min_ps/_mm256_max_ps, or the _mm512 versions when CPUID reports AVX-512F; _mm256_min_epi16 for int16), followed by a horizontal reduction and a pairwise scalar tail. On large arrays the workload is memory-bound, so reading the data once instead of twice is the bulk of the claimed 2.3x. 1-D strided float32 is packed into vectors with _mm256_set_ps, which the comments say beat hardware gather.
when_to_use: Large contiguous float32 buffers (audio frames, images, sensor dumps) on Linux x86-64 where you need both extremes and the data is known to be finite: one memory pass instead of two.
Contiguous int16 PCM audio on Linux x86-64 with AVX2.
1-D strided float32 views such as one channel of interleaved audio (a[::n]), which NumPy reduces with two strided passes.
Projects pinned to NumPy 2.0-2.5, which have no single-pass min/max; NumPy 2.6 adds np.minmax.
when_not_to_use: Data that can contain NaN or consist only of infinities: results can be silently wrong (see gotchas). np.amin/np.amax propagate NaN; np.nanmin/np.nanmax ignore it.

NumPy 2.6 or later: np.minmax (numpy/numpy PR #32231, merged 2026-09-10) does the same single pass for every dtype, with axis support and NaN propagation. A NumPy maintainer measured 9.15 ms vs 17.7 ms for min+max on 1e8 float64 values.

Windows, macOS or ARM wheels: the published win_amd64 0.6.0 wheel contains only the scalar pairwise loop (no AVX instructions in the binary), the macOS wheels are arm64-only, and ARM has no NEON path (issue #18), so the advertised AVX speedup exists only in the Linux x86-64 wheels.
Many tiny arrays: constant cffi and Python dispatch cost dominates (issue #16: 9-element and 23-element arrays take about the same time), and no small-array win is published.
float64, other integer types, N-D strided arrays or per-axis reductions: these take the np.amin + np.amax fallback, plus wrapper overhead.

integration.form: module (PyPI wheels built with cffi; the C kernel is a single _minmax.c file of about 300 lines that can be vendored)
integration.min_toolchain: CPython 3.10-3.14, including free-threaded 3.14t wheels; numpy 2.x (use a pre-0.4.0 release for numpy 1.x); an sdist build on x86 needs a compiler that accepts -mavx -mavx512f (Linux wheels use clang)
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux: every float32 call needs AVX, the int16 path needs AVX2, and AVX-512F is used when detected. aarch64 Linux, macOS arm64 and the Windows x86-64 wheel: scalar only. No Windows arm64 build (issue #31).
integration.thread_safety: not documented. The C kernels keep no global mutable state, cffi releases the GIL around the call (PyEval_SaveThread in the 0.6.0 Linux wheel), and cp314t wheels are published, so concurrent calls on arrays that are not being mutated look safe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — returns the same (min, max) as (np.amin(a), np.amax(a)) for finite float32 and int16 data, but has no axis, keepdims, out, where or initial arguments, and differs from NumPy on NaN and all-infinity inputs

gotchas: NaN corrupts results instead of propagating. MINPS returns its second operand when either input is NaN, so a NaN lane overwrites the accumulated minimum and the next chunk replaces it. In the scalar pairwise code a NaN knocks its pair partner out of the comparison. Emulating the exact C logic: 32 float32 values with -5 at index 0 and NaN at index 16 give (1.0, 1.0) on the AVX-512 path, [0, NaN, 5, 6] gives (5, 6), [1, 2, 3, NaN] gives (NaN, NaN), and 32 NaNs give (3.4028235e38, -3.4028235e38). Each case matches neither np.amin (NaN) nor np.nanmin. The tests have no NaN case; open issue #38 only asks for nanmax-style behaviour.

The SIMD accumulators start at FLT_MAX and -FLT_MAX instead of the first element or infinity. A float32 array of 16 or more +inf values whose length is a multiple of the vector width (16 with AVX-512, 8 with AVX) returns min = 3.4028235e38 instead of inf; all -inf returns max = -3.4028235e38.

A 1-D float32 view with stride 0 and at least 16 elements, such as np.broadcast_to(np.float32(1), (16,)) (C_CONTIGUOUS False, strides (0,)), sends x86-64 into minmax_avx_strided_float32, whose loop step is 8*stride = 0, so the call never returns. The GIL is released during the hang.

ISA dispatch is fragile. The AVX path and the AVX2 int16 path run without any CPUID check (SIGILL on x86-64 CPUs lacking them). The AVX-512 check runs CPUID leaf 7 on every call of 16 or more elements without setting ECX, because the code uses __cpuid rather than __cpuid_count, so the subleaf is whatever the register holds. Detection can silently miss AVX-512, and under virtualization every call pays a CPUID VM exit. On the positive side, the 0.6.0 cp312 manylinux wheel confines zmm code to minmax_avx512_float32.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over argminmax (Rust, returns indices, has NaN-aware variants and runtime SIMD dispatch including NEON) only when you are in Python, need the values for NaN-free float32 or int16 data on Linux x86-64, and cannot move to NumPy 2.6's np.minmax. vstat covers wider descriptive statistics from C++.
verified_claims_summary: The README gives one figure, roughly 2.3x over np.amin followed by np.amax, on an unnamed Intel CPU with numpy 1.24-1.26; no table or output is published. scripts/perf_benchmark.py times numpy's pair once and minmax as the median of 5 with time.time() (diplib is a third arm), over 100,000 9-element and 3x9 arrays and over arrays of about 1e9 float32 elements (1-D, 2-D C/F, flipped, stride 5). Issue #15 concedes each test runs one iteration with notable variation on small arrays. The large-array gain is what fusing two memory-bound passes into one predicts, and none of the benchmark inputs contain NaN or infinity.
status_note: Lightly maintained by Nomono (0.6.0 tagged 2025-12-27, wheels for CPython 3.10-3.14 uploaded 2026-06-26, last commit a 2026-06-04 dependency bump), MIT and labelled alpha. The 2.3x is an unpublished one-iteration numpy-1.x figure; SIMD exists only in the Linux x86-64 wheels; NaN, all-infinity and stride-0 inputs give wrong results or hang; and NumPy 2.6's np.minmax will cover the same use upstream.
